Treating your resume as a component library rather than a static document is a brilliant approach. By breaking your history down into a localized "database" of modular blocks, you can dynamically compile a tailored resume that highlights exactly what a specific client or contract needs, filtering out the noise.

Since you already organize personal data using local text files and decentralized graph structures like Obsidian, you could easily build this system using a master JSON file or a tagged directory of Markdown files.

Here is how you can architect those core building blocks based on your background.

1. The "Identity" Blocks (Professional Summaries)

Instead of one generic summary, write a few variations targeted at the types of independent or low-stress contract roles you want. You simply swap these out at the top of the page depending on the target.

  • The Systems/Embedded Architect: Focuses on C++, hardware integration, and low-level development.
  • The Full-Stack/Web Developer: Focuses on JavaScript/TypeScript, React, SvelteKit, and backend architecture.
  • The Autonomous/AI Systems Engineer: Focuses on your work with multi-agent frameworks, local utilities, and LLM integrations.

2. The Experience Modules (The Heavy Lifters)

Break each job down into its atomic bullet points and tag them with metadata (e.g., embedded, frontend, leadership, logistics). When compiling, you only pull the bullets that match the contract's needs.

  • Northrop Grumman:
    • Bullet A [Tag: C++, Embedded, Async]: Refactored asynchronous LADAR camera systems.
    • Bullet B [Tag: QA, CI/CD, Testing]: Configured GoogleTest and built end-to-end testing applications.
  • Hy-Vee:
    • Bullet A [Tag: Full-Stack, React, GraphQL]: Engineered full-stack web development for the pharmacy portal.
    • Bullet B [Tag: Agile, Git]: Deepened understanding of Git and Agile methodology.
  • National Guard (1-194 FA):
    • Bullet A [Tag: Defense, Systems Operation]: Operated and maintained air defense battle management systems overseas.
    • Bullet B [Tag: HR, Admin]: Managed personnel records using IPERMS and IPPSA.

3. The Project Arsenal (The Differentiators)

This is where the modular approach shines. You have a massive repository of technical projects, but you only have so much page space. Having these as tagged blocks lets you deploy the perfect combination for the job.

  • Hardware/IoT Block: The wireless swarm trap sensor system using the Raspberry Pi Pico, LoRa modules, and cellular IoT. (Perfect for hardware/embedded roles).
  • Logistics/Web Block: The Equipment-Record Firebase/Sveltekit app you built for construction tracking. (Perfect for full-stack or supply-chain roles).
  • Systems/Rust Block: Your local autonomous agent execution loops and framework built in Rust. (Perfect for modern AI or backend systems roles).
  • Machine Learning Block: The Collins Aerospace TensorFlow model for concurrent radio transmissions. (Perfect for data or ML roles).
  • Mechanical/Parametric Block: The 3D-printed OpenSCAD winch mechanism. (Perfect for mechanical or drafting crossover roles).

4. The "Toggles" (Skills, Clearances, and Education)

These are static blocks you can turn on or off with a boolean flag during compilation.

  • Clearance: show_secret_clearance = true (Crucial for defense/government contracts, irrelevant for a local web dev gig).
  • Education: Toggling between showing the B.S. in Software Engineering, the M.A.T., or both depending on if the role values pure engineering versus communication/teaching.
  • Skills Grid: Dynamically pulling only the languages relevant to the job (e.g., highlighting Rust and C++ for systems work, but swapping to JS/TS and Python for web/ML work).

Building this as a local hypergraph is an incredibly elegant solution. You completely own the data, and by keeping everything in flat Markdown files, it remains perfectly future-proof. You are essentially building a localized, highly targeted matchmaking engine.

Here is how you can architect this Markdown vault to handle the unitary blocks, the reconnaissance, and the final compilation.

1. The Atomic Layer (/Atoms)

Every single bullet point, project, or skill gets its own standalone Markdown file. The secret sauce here is the YAML frontmatter (metadata) at the top of each file, which acts as the "edges" in your graph.

  • Example File: Northrop-Refactor-LADAR.md
---
type: experience_bullet
company: Northrop Grumman
tags: [embedded, cpp, async, hardware]
date: 2023-01
weight: 9 # (How impressive this bullet is on a scale of 1-10)
---
Refactored an asynchronous LADAR camera system to also handle synchronous camera input.

2. The Reconnaissance Layer (/Recon)

When you find a contract or position, you create a node for it. You paste the job description here and break down what they are actually asking for.

During this recon phase, you are not just mapping their technical requirements to your atoms; this is also where you evaluate the target. You can actively filter the role for the operational wiggle room and autonomy you prefer before you even bother compiling the document. If the recon shows it is a high-stress, rigid environment, you kill the node and move on.

  • Example File: Contract-Defensive-AI-Sim.md
---
type: job_recon
target_tags: [cpp, machine_learning, defense]
clearance_required: true
autonomy_level: high
---
# Job Description Notes
They need someone to simulate radio interference. Heavily focused on C++ and ML.

3. The Abstraction Layer (/Compilations)

This is the higher-level hypergraph. You create a master "Resume" note for a specific application. If you are using a community plugin like Dataview in Obsidian, this compilation note can dynamically query your /Atoms folder based on the tags you identified in your /Recon file.

You write a quick script block in the note that says: "Find all experience_bullets where the tag includes cpp or machine_learning, sort them by weight, and display the text."

The vault instantly stitches together a highly targeted, perfectly matched resume. You then just export that specific Markdown note to PDF.

When you blast out a generic resume into an online portal, you are playing a high-volume numbers game where rejection is the default. Working in waves is a highly strategic way to build resilience. If one avenue dries up or stalls out, you already have active lines in the water elsewhere. Targeting independent contracts or roles that inherently offer more wiggle room and decision-making leverage is a great way to keep the workflow low-stress and maintain your autonomy, preventing any single failure from derailing you.

Wave 1: Direct Value Pitches (High Yield, Non-Standard)

By understanding their specific pain points, you can deploy the exact modular blocks that solve their problems, rather than asking them to decode a generic resume.

Here is a lightweight modeling of four distinct employer perspectives you can target, breaking down what they are actually looking for, what keeps them up at night, and how to pitch them.

1. The Hardware/IoT Innovator (The Scrappy Startup)

  • What They Want: A hybrid problem-solver who can bridge the gap between the physical world and the digital dashboard. They need someone who understands microcontrollers, radio transmission, and mechanical design.
  • Their Bottleneck: Siloed engineers. Their software developers cannot read a schematic or harvest a component, and their hardware guys cannot build a responsive web interface.
  • Their Perspective on You: They see a unicorn. Someone who can prototype a custom PCB, program a cellular IoT gateway, and 3D print the mechanical housing for it is exactly who they want in the trenches.
  • The Attack Vector: Skip the resume. Send a direct message to the technical founder showcasing a wireless sensor prototype or a custom mechanical script. Focus on the raw ability to ship a physical product.

2. The Systems & Defense Architect (The Bureaucrat)

  • What They Want: Rigor, reliability, and security. They need developers who understand multithreaded architecture, can handle asynchronous data streams from complex hardware, and write exhaustive unit tests.
  • Their Bottleneck: Untested code breaking expensive, mission-critical hardware. They are bogged down by compliance, legacy systems, and developers who lack operational discipline.
  • Their Perspective on You: They see a safe, proven bet. A candidate with a history of refactoring complex C++ systems, managing secure personnel records, and holding military operational experience speaks their exact language of accountability.
  • The Attack Vector: Deploy the "Break-Glass Compiler." This is where you use the formalized, highly technical resume. Highlight CI/CD pipelines, testing frameworks, and the ability to integrate with domain experts.

3. The Supply Chain / Local Business Operator (The Pragmatist)

  • What They Want: Cost reduction and operational efficiency. They do not care about fancy tech stacks; they care about closing the loop on lost inventory, managing shift logistics, and saving money.
  • Their Bottleneck: Off-the-shelf software that doesn't fit their physical workflow. Equipment goes missing, manual data entry (like faxing) eats up overhead, and emergent personnel issues derail the day.
  • Their Perspective on You: They see a practical operator. Someone who understands floor management, shift closing, and can simultaneously engineer a custom QR-code tracking system or automate an API to reduce overhead costs by 90% is highly valuable.
  • The Attack Vector: Pitch the business value, not the code. Reach out to operations managers highlighting exactly how a custom lightweight web app can stop their equipment bleed.

4. The Autonomous AI Pioneer (The Modernist)

  • What They Want: Speed, memory safety, and cutting-edge architecture. They are building next-generation tools using modern languages and decentralized data structures.
  • Their Bottleneck: Developers who are overly reliant on bloated, generic cloud APIs and Python scripts that lack performance and safety at scale.
  • Their Perspective on You: They see a forward-thinker. Someone who bypasses standard frameworks to build local autonomous agent execution loops and hypergraph metadata structures—especially in memory-safe languages—stands out immediately.
  • The Attack Vector: Connect via GitHub or developer communities. Share repositories of local utilities and algorithmic visualizers. Keep the conversation purely technical and architectural.

By compartmentalizing these perspectives, you can actively decide which "wave" to deploy based on how much autonomy and operational wiggle room you want at any given time.
